learningObjectives.title: The causes of war and Just War theory

questions.q: Which early Christian thinker is often credited with helping to develop the idea of a Just War?
questions.explain: Augustine of Hippo is traditionally regarded as an early Christian source for Just War thinking, later refined by Aquinas.

questions.q: Which medieval theologian set out key conditions for a just war in his Summa Theologica?
questions.explain: Thomas Aquinas outlined conditions such as legitimate authority, just cause and right intention for a war to be just.

questions.q: Which of the following is a traditional condition for beginning a just war (jus ad bellum)?
options: The war must be a last resort
The war must use nuclear weapons
The war must be fought in secret
The war must last less than a year
questions.explain: War may only be just if all peaceful options have first been exhausted, making it a genuine last resort.

questions.q: What does the Just War condition of 'proportionality' mean?
options: The good expected must outweigh the harm caused
Only the strongest army is allowed to fight
Every soldier must be a volunteer
The war must be declared on television
questions.explain: Proportionality requires that the benefits of going to (or fighting a) war are greater than the suffering it causes.

questions.q: The principle of 'discrimination' in fighting a just war (jus in bello) requires that:
options: civilians and non-combatants must not be deliberately targeted
soldiers may choose their own enemies
only professional armies are allowed to fight
weapons must be shared equally between sides
questions.explain: Discrimination means fighters must distinguish combatants from innocent civilians, who must not be attacked.

questions.q: Which Christian group, also known as the Religious Society of Friends, is strongly associated with pacifism?
questions.explain: The Quakers (Religious Society of Friends) are well known for their long-standing commitment to peace and pacifism.

options: The belief that violence and war are never justified under any circumstances
The belief that war is always acceptable in self-defence
The belief that only nuclear war is wrong
The belief that soldiers should be well paid
questions.explain: Absolute pacifists reject all use of violence and war, whatever the situation or supposed benefit.

questions.q: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus said, 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called...' what?
questions.explain: This teaching from Matthew's Gospel is often used by Christians to support working actively for peace.

questions.q: Which teaching of Jesus is most often used to support non-violence?
options: 'A time for war and a time for peace'
questions.explain: 'Turn the other cheek' encourages a response of non-retaliation rather than returning violence with violence.

options: The restoring of friendly relations after conflict
The punishing of those who have done wrong
The declaring of war on an enemy
The refusing to forgive an offender
questions.explain: Reconciliation is bringing together people who were opposed and rebuilding a broken relationship.

questions.q: In a religious context, 'justice' is best described as:
options: bringing about what is right and fair for all
ignoring the needs of the poor
questions.explain: Justice concerns fairness and putting right what is wrong, and is valued by many believers as a duty.

questions.q: Why might many Christians see forgiveness as important for peace?
options: It can break the cycle of revenge and allow relationships to be restored
It guarantees material wealth to those who forgive
It removes the need for any laws in society
It forces enemies to change their religion
questions.explain: Forgiveness can stop repeated cycles of retaliation and open the way to reconciliation and peace.

questions.q: A Christian refuses to join the army because they believe all killing is wrong, even in a war of self-defence. Which position best describes them?
questions.explain: Rejecting all violence in every circumstance, including self-defence, is the position of absolute pacifism.

questions.q: Which of the following is commonly identified as a cause of war?
questions.explain: Competition for territory and resources is a frequently cited cause of conflict between groups and nations.

questions.q: What is meant by a 'holy war'?
options: A war fought for a religious cause, often believed to be supported by God
A war fought only with non-lethal weapons
A war fought between two churches over money
Any war involving more than two nations
questions.explain: A holy war is fought to defend or promote a religion and is often seen by its supporters as sanctioned by God.

questions.q: A country invades a peaceful neighbour purely to seize its oil fields. Which Just War condition is most clearly broken?
questions.explain: Attacking simply to seize resources is not a just cause, since there is no genuine wrong being put right.

questions.q: What distinguishes 'contingent (conditional) pacifism' from absolute pacifism?
options: It opposes war in most cases but accepts it could be justified in some circumstances
It supports all wars without question
It applies only to religious believers
questions.explain: Contingent pacifists generally reject war but may allow that it could be justified, for example in defence against great evil.

questions.q: After a civil war, a country sets up a commission where victims and offenders meet, share their experiences and rebuild trust. This best illustrates:
questions.explain: Bringing former enemies together to restore trust and relationships is an example of reconciliation.

questions.q: A believer joins a peaceful protest march against the arms trade rather than using force. This action best reflects:
questions.explain: Peaceful protest expresses opposition without violence, reflecting a commitment to non-violent means of change.
